subtopics.title: Charges Must Cancel — the One Law of Formula Writing

questions.question: The one law governing every ionic formula is:
options: The compound must be electrically neutral — total positive and negative charges cancel
Every formula needs exactly two elements

questions.question: A group two metal like calcium forms an ion with charge:
Why does magnesium chloride need TWO chlorides (MgCl2)?
options: One Cl⁻ cannot cancel Mg's 2+ charge, but two can

subtopics.title: Calcium Chloride and the Crossover Method

questions.question: The formula for calcium chloride is:
In the crossover method, the numbers that cross over are:
options: The sizes of the charges, each becoming the OTHER ion's subscript

questions.question: Crossing Mg²⁺ with O²⁻ gives Mg2O2. The correct final formula is:
options: MgO — subscripts must be simplified to the smallest ratio
Mg2O2 — the crossover result is always final

questions.question: The charge audit for CaCl2 confirms neutrality because:
options: Calcium and chlorine are in the same period
One Ca at 2+ gives +2 and two Cl at 1− give −2, summing to zero

subtopics.title: Ammonium Sulphate — Polyatomic Ions and the Bracket Rule

questions.question: The ammonium and sulphate ions are:
The formula for ammonium sulphate is:
Brackets are required in (NH4)2SO4 because:
options: The subscript 2 must multiply the whole ammonium team — without brackets the formula miscounts atoms
Sulphate demands brackets around its partner
Brackets make the formula look neater

subtopics.title: Iron(III) Oxide — Roman Numerals and the Complete Method

questions.question: The Roman numeral in 'iron(III) oxide' tells you:
options: The iron ion carries a 3+ charge
It is the third oxide discovered

questions.question: The formula for iron(III) oxide is:
Why do transition metals like iron need Roman numerals when group one metals do not?
options: Group one metals have no charge
It is a historical accident with no meaning
Transition metals can form more than one ion (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺), so the name must specify which

questions.question: Iron(II) oxide and iron(III) oxide are:
options: The same compound written two ways
Different compounds — FeO and Fe2O3 — with different properties

questions.question: In the till analogy, the metals are the 'givers'. What does giving electrons away leave a metal atom as?
Calcium hands out 2 and each chloride takes only 1. The mix that closes the till at zero is:
Why is Mg2O2 the wrong way to write magnesium oxide, even though the charges do cancel?
options: The charges do not actually cancel
The ratio 2 : 2 must be cancelled down to 1 : 1, giving MgO

subtopics.title: The Team Rides in One Taxi

questions.question: In the taxi picture, what do the brackets in (NH4)2SO4 represent?
options: The taxi that carries the whole ammonium group so it can be doubled as one unit
The charge on the sulphate ion
A reminder that nitrogen is a gas

questions.question: Why does sulphate get no brackets in ammonium sulphate?
options: Sulphate is not a polyatomic ion
Only one sulphate is present, so no subscript has to multiply it
Sulphate is negative and negatives never take brackets
Brackets are only ever used once per formula

questions.question: The name endings '-ide' and '-ate' tell you that:
options: '-ide' means the ion is positive and '-ate' means it is negative
Both endings mean exactly the same thing
'-ide' is a lone atom ion (S²⁻) while '-ate' is a group with oxygens aboard (SO4²⁻)
'-ate' ions never appear on the data sheet

subtopics.title: When the Name Whispers the Charge

questions.question: Iron hands out 3 and oxygen takes 2. The smallest number both fit into is 6, which gives the everyday substance rust as:
Which step of the five-step recipe is the 'count the till' step?
options: Finding the ratio by swapping numbers
The final audit: pluses against minuses, and atoms counted with brackets respected

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four common ways learners lose the mark?
options: Using the data sheet to look up a polyatomic ion's charge
Crossing over and forgetting to cancel down
Leaving the brackets out of an ammonium formula
Ignoring the Roman numeral and writing FeO for iron(III) oxide
